articles.title: Tulip Siddiq says she is considering legal action against former Bangladesh leader
articles.summary: Former minister, who was sentenced to prison in Bangladesh in her absence, says she was victim of ‘malicious prosecution’
body: The former minister Tulip Siddiq has said she is considering taking legal action against the former interim leader of Bangladesh over corruption allegations made by his administration that led her to resign from the UK government last year.

The MP for Hampstead and Highgate, whose aunt Sheikh Hasina was put on trial in absentia over crimes against humanity during her 15 years as prime minister of Bangladesh, was accused of benefiting from the former regime by the authorities in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka.

Siddiq was sentenced to two years in prison in Bangladesh in December last year after being put on trial in her absence, alongside 16 other people, over corruption allegations. She was found guilty of influencing her aunt to secure a plot of land for her family in the outskirts of Dhaka. Siddiq, who is based in London and strongly denied the charges, is unlikely to ever serve the sentence.

In an interview with the Guardian in summer 2025, Siddiq called the charges against her “completely absurd”, saying she was “collateral damage” in a longstanding feud between her aunt and Bangladesh’s former interim leader Muhammad Yunus.

Speaking to Politics Unleashed – a new podcast hosted by Guto Harri and David Davis – Siddiq said she had been the victim of a “malicious prosecution”. She added that she was speaking with a reputable lawyer who had told her she had a case to sue Yunus, the Nobel peace prize-winning economist who led the interim government in Bangladesh from 2024 to 2026.
“It was essentially malicious prosecution,” she said, adding that she was exploring options with lawyers and “considering” legal action.
Yunus, approached for a response through two close associates, declined to comment.
Siddiq said she had repeatedly tried to get details about what she was accused of, but the Bangladesh government had not replied to letters from her lawyers.

She detailed sending a handwritten letter to Yunus, who was staying at the Dorchester in London. “He refused to meet with me. I tried repeatedly to see him face to face,” she said, insisting she had not been stressed by the accusations and subsequent trial because she knew she was innocent. “I was more baffled by the whole thing than anything else,” she said.

Speaking about the impact of the trial, she compared the experience to being in a “Kafkaesque nightmare”, adding: “I had no idea what I was being convicted for. The only way I found out I had been convicted is when I woke up in the morning and saw an alert from Sky News.”

Siddiq also revealed she had received support from the former prime minister Keir Starmer during the controversy. She said he sent her a message when he was in the US with Donald Trump after she had received a security threat. “It kind of matched with the timing of when he was just about to see Trump,” she said.

But when Starmer was asked repeatedly about Siddiq, she decided she had to resign. She said: “I had been part of the project to get Keir into No 10. I had supported him from the beginning … and then here I am, being the obstacle.”
The Starmer loyalist said the toppling of the former prime minister was “very painful”, but praised his successor, Andy Burnham.

“At the end of the day, what I want is a Labour government, another Labour government,” she said. “If Andy is going to deliver that, then I have to put my sadness aside and focus on the fact that we have a Labour government that’s doing well in the polls.”

articles.title: Datacentres to create 70% more carbon emissions by 2030, IEA report warns
articles.summary: Global energy watchdog forecasts huge rise as US and China turn to fossil fuels to power AI growth agendas
body: The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four years as the US and China turn to fossil fuels to power their AI growth agendas, according to the world’s energy watchdog.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that datacentres will consume twice as much electricity by 2030 compared with today, with the global expansion of artificial intelligence accounting for three-quarters of this growth.

The Paris-based agency found that the breakneck pace of the industry’s growth means that within four years AI datacentres will consume an extra 350 terrawatt-hours of electricity every year, or more than the annual electricity consumption of Great Britain.

Its influential annual report warned that the world’s energy future was less certain after the impact of the Middle East war, which it has described as the greatest energy market disruption in history.
“I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” said the IEA’s executive director Fatih Birol.

Instead, it will be reshaped by the policy decisions governments make after the crisis to meet the increasing demand for energy to power a growing global population, the rising need for air-conditioning and a booming AI economy, the IEA said.

Datacentre developers have emerged as the world’s biggest corporate buyers of renewable energy to help fuel their servers which have a connection to local power grids. Despite this, the report showed that the appetite for fossil fuels is expected to grow even faster, particularly in the US and China.

By the end of the decade, around half of the electricity needed to power China’s AI datacentres will come from coal power plants, according to the IEA. The rest will come from renewable energy, with smaller amounts from nuclear reactors and very little from gas plants.

In contrast, the US is expected to rely on gas to provide about 60% of the electricity for its datacentres by 2030. There were plans for about 180GW of new gas-fired power plants linked to US datacentres in August this year, the agency said. That is almost as much new gas capacity as the total now installed across the European Union.
As a result of the growth in fossil fuel generation for datacentres, emissions associated with this sector were on track to rise by 70% by 2030, the IEA said.

The appetite for gas power among US datacentre developers is more than 16 times higher than in Canada, where the IEA identified plans for 11GW of gas generation to power their servers. In the rest of the world, AI developers have put forward plans for new gas plants with a combined capacity of just 4GW, the agency said.

This is because renewable energy is expected to play a greater role in supplying datacentres outside the US and China. In the EU, the IEA expects datacentres to rely on renewables for about 70% of their electricity by 2030 – followed by nuclear power, gas generation, and a very small amount of coal power.

The agency based its forecasts for the notoriously opaque industry on data showing the annual global shipment of AI servers, which have climbed eighteen-fold since 2020. It also used space-based imagery to track the buildout of 93 large “AI factories” around the world.

Its analysis suggests that the world’s datacentre capacity has climbed tenfold in the last 24 months to 17GW. By the time the AI factories were completed, their combined capacity was likely to be about 50GW, the IEA said.

The world’s existing stock of datacentres, including those with AI-optimised servers, now stands at 120GW, with 80% of this capacity in China, the US and the EU. A further 120GW will be built by the end of the decade under the IEA scenario often considered its central base case, of which three-quarters will be AI datacentres.

articles.title: China gives Japan PM frosty welcome at Apec amid fanfare for other leaders
articles.summary: Sanae Takaichi cuts lonely figure at airport, a move by China that is being linked to the simmering row over Taiwan
body: Apec’s Chinese hosts went out of their way to give world leaders a warm welcome as they arrived in Shenzhen this week. Military bands played, dozens of cheering young men and women waved colourful bouquets, and senior officials offered hugs and handshakes on the tarmac.
But there was one exception: Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi.

The red carpet was rolled out for her arrival at Shenzhen Bao’an International Airport, but Takaichi, on her first visit to China since taking office just over a year ago, had to make do with a modest guard of honour and a welcome from a relatively junior Chinese government official.
Related: Hi-tech Shenzhen takes centre stage as Xi sends ‘Chinamaxxing’ message at Apec summit

The contrast in hospitality was impossible to ignore. Donald Trump was personally greeted by Chinese leader Xi Jinping as he stepped off Air Force One, while Vladimir Putin was met by Cai Qi, a senior Communist party official and one of Xi’s closest aides.

The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, beamed as he walked past rows of women in white shirts and pink skirts while soldiers from the People’s Liberation Army stood to attention, bayonets fixed. South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, and the country’s first lady, Kim Hea Kyung, were given similar VIP treatment.

Takaichi, on the other hand, was met off her plane by Zhang Qiyue, China’s former ambassador to Greece, a position below those who greeted other leaders. Zhang, though, does have a connection with Japan: her father, Zhang Shu, was once China’s ambassador in Tokyo.

Many are linking China’s frosty welcome to a simmering row over Taiwan that began shortly after Takaichi made her diplomatic debut at the 2025 Apec summit in South Korea, where she and Xi vowed to build “constructive and stable” relations.

Less than a fortnight later, Takaichi triggered a diplomatic crisis when she told MPs that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could trigger the deployment of her country’s self-defence forces if the conflict posed an existential threat to Japan, whose westernmost island, Yonaguni, is just 100km from Taiwan.
Insisting that Japan could exercise its right to collective self-defence – or coming to the aid of an ally, namely the US – Takaichi said Tokyo had to plan for a crisis in the Taiwan strait.
Beijing has not ruled out the use of force to annex Taiwan – a self-governing democracy it regards as a Chinese province – under what it calls “reunification”.
China’s foreign ministry condemned her remarks at the time as “wrongful and dangerous,” while online, many accused Japan’s leader of dragging her country back into prewar militarism.

The dispute soured economic and cultural ties. Beijing warned Chinese citizens not to take holidays or study in Japan, claiming, without evidence, that they would face threats to their safety. Grassroots exchanges were called off and the Chinese releases of Japanese films postponed indefinitely.

Panda diplomacy also took a hit in January, when Xiao Xiao and Lei Lei, a pair of giant pandas that had been kept at Ueno Zoo in Tokyo, departed Japan, leaving the country without one of the animals for the first time since 1972, when Tokyo and Beijing normalised diplomatic ties.

As Xi, Trump and Putin prepared to hold historic three-way talks in Shenzhen on Thursday, Takaichi managed only a cordial handshake and a few words with Xi – another reminder that Japan-China relations have yet to come in from the cold.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Russia asks if Netherlands has joined conflict after Crimea bridge strike
articles.summary: Russian embassy reacts to use of missiles made by Dutch-based company in Tuesday’s Kerch bridge attack. What we know on day 1,730
body: Russia’s embassy in the Netherlands has posted a statement asking if the Netherlands had openly joined ⁠the conflict ⁠in ​Ukraine after a Dutch-based company said its missiles ⁠were used by Kyiv in Tuesday’s attack on a Crimean bridge. A section ​of the Kerch bridge that ‌connects annexed Crimea and Russia was destroyed on Tuesday by waves of ⁠drones and missiles. Soon after, Destinus – a Dutch-headquartered startup – confirmed its Ruta cruise missiles ‌were the only foreign-made weapons used in the attack, a rare operational role for a western manufacturer in a significant long-range strike.

In response to the revelation, the ​Russian embassy said on X that “Moscow has ⁠been duly informed of the NL (Netherlands) involvement”, above a ​statement from ‌Destinus detailing ​its ​role in the bridge attack. The embassy added: “The confession has been well noted. Is The Hague openly joining the conflict?”

In a separate strike on Wednesday, the bridge was attacked again, temporarily halting traffic. “An assessment of the damage is under way,” Sergei Aksyonov, the Moscow-appointed head of Crimea, wrote on Telegram. For Ukraine, the bridge is a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Ukraine has previously declared that the bridge across the Kerch strait, built eight years ago, is illegal. The strike came hours ahead of a meeting between Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping at Apec in China.

Trump plans to meet separately with Putin on Thursday, in addition to their already scheduled three-way meeting with Xi, a US official confirmed. Trump’s meeting with Putin would be the first time that the leaders have held talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal to ease Russia’s war in Ukraine.

A Russian man has been arrested in California for allegedly conducting surveillance of employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defence company that provided assistance to Ukraine, US officials said. The targeted company was not named in the indictment but it was described as a “large, publicly traded” technology and defence company with office locations throughout the US, including in Palo Alto.

Ukraine struck two oil refineries in southern Russia overnight, Ukrainian officials said on Wednesday. Ukraine’s general staff said the strikes hit storage tanks at the Ilsky refinery and a processing unit at the Afipsky refinery, both in Russia’s Krasnodar region. The two refineries, also targeted Sunday night, could together process about 95m barrels of oil a year and supply Russian forces on the frontlines in southern and eastern Ukraine, it said.

Russian drones attacked energy facilities, civilian businesses and residential buildings in five regions overnight and Wednesday morning, Ukrainian prime minister Serhii Koretskyi said. A Russian strike on the southern Ukrainian city of Odesa killed four people, officials said. A Russian drone attack on a market in the Kharkiv region wounded 12 people, including an 11-year-old boy, Ukraine’s State Emergency Services said.

The EU has proposed member states give Ukraine an extra €45bn ($49bn) loan to plug its 2027 budget shortfalls as Russia’s invasion drags on, Jennifer Rankin writes. The funding would fill two-thirds of a €70bn black hole Kyiv faces next year. “We think this is the best way to give Ukraine a strong hand at the negotiation table, and Ukraine only needs to repay once Russia pays for the damage it has caused in Ukraine,” European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen said. EU leaders will discuss the loan next week.

US diplomatic envoys Steve Witkoff and ⁠Jared Kushner are expected in Berlin on Thursday to meet Ukrainian officials and a European negotiating team, a US official said. The meetings would focus on further developing “credible postwar security guarantees” ⁠for Ukraine, and preparing for the next round of multilateral talks, the official said.

Russian ⁠athletes will not be allowed into ⁠the ⁠Czech Republic, ​which is hosting ⁠the women’s under-18 ice hockey world championship ⁠in January. In comments to local media, interior minister ‌Lubomir Metnar ‌reiterated his government would not ‌be issuing visas for Russian ​athletes. He added that the ministry also had ⁠legal instruments to ​prevent entry for ​athletes ​receiving visas from ​other ‌states ​in ​Europe’s border-free Schengen zone.
